cards.title: Introduction to Java Syntax
cards.content:
Every Java program must have at least one class definition and a main method. Java is case-sensitive, and every statement must end with a semicolon.

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, World!");
    }
}

cards.title: Variables and Primitive Data Types
cards.content:
Java is statically-typed, meaning variables must be declared with a data type before they can be used. Java provides primitive types (such as int, double, char, boolean) and reference types (such as String, arrays, and objects).

int age = 25;
double price = 19.99;
char grade = 'A';
boolean isJavaFun = true;

content.text: To prevent a variable from being reassigned (making it a constant), you must use the [blank] keyword in Java syntax.

cards.title: Java Operators
cards.content:
Operators perform operations on variables and values. Java includes:

  • Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, %
  • Relational: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=
  • Logical: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)

cards.title: Control Flow: Conditionals
cards.content:
Conditional statements allow your program to execute different code blocks based on conditions using if, else if, else, and switch structures.

int score = 85;
if (score >= 90) {
    System.out.println("Grade: A");
} else if (score >= 80) {
    System.out.println("Grade: B");
} else {
    System.out.println("Grade: C");
}

content.instructions: Arrange the code blocks to form a logically structured conditional check that executes starting with the highest check.

cards.title: Control Flow: Loops
cards.content:
Loops execute a block of code repeatedly. Java supports for loops, while loops, and do-while loops.

// For loop
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

// While loop
int x = 0;
while (x < 5) {
    System.out.println(x);
    x++;
}

cards.title: Comments and Naming Conventions
cards.content:
Java comments can be single-line (//) or multi-line (/* ... */). Additionally, Java developers follow naming conventions:

  • Classes: PascalCase (e.g., MyService)
  • Variables & Methods: camelCase (e.g., calculateTotalValue())
  • Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., MAX_LIMIT)

cards.title: Syntax Essentials Summary
cards.content: To summarize, writing clean Java requires keeping statements terminated with semicolons, establishing precise type constraints, writing structured condition checks and loop statements, and styling code following PascalCase for classes and camelCase for methods and variables.
